## Development validation

This vignette accompanies development version 0.99.2.
The benchmark covers selected configurations, and the validation study uses
100 datasets per metric with 99 resampling draws. These small simulations
provide diagnostics; they do not establish general statistical calibration.
The local study observed 24% peak false positives, 10% peak detection,
74.9% transfer interval coverage, and 43% drift interval coverage in the
tested scenarios. These results limit inferential use of these methods. Report sources are `scripts/benchmark.R` and `scripts/validate.R`.

## What crossStatR is for

crossStatR is a statistics toolkit for bench scientists who work with
quantitative experimental data: enzyme kinetics, dose-response curves,
cyclic voltammetry, UV-Vis and Raman spectra, calibration curves,
exponential decay experiments. The package collects the methods
bench scientists reach for repeatedly, with three commitments that guide its design.

The package is conservative by default. It does not silently remove
observations, it does not pick a hypothesis test on the basis of a
normality-test p-value, and it distinguishes biological from
technical replicates in its variance models. Pre-testing for normality
and switching tests on the result inflates Type I error (Rochon,
Gondan and Kieser, 2012); pseudo-replication produces confidence
intervals that are far too narrow (Vaux, Fidler and Cumming, 2012).
crossStatR avoids both by construction.

The package separates biological and technical variation. When the analyst supplies
`sci_describe()` which column identifies biological replicates and which
identifies technical replicates, the function averages technical
replicates within each biological unit *before* computing summary
statistics. The reported `n` then refers to biological replicates.

The package documents its own limitations. Every function carries a
Limitations section in its help page, and the Category C methods (the
advanced uncertainty-attribution tools) are explicit about when their
assumptions break.

## Installation

The development version can be installed from
[R-universe](https://rotsl.r-universe.dev/crossStatR):

```{r install-runiverse, eval = FALSE}
install.packages(
  "crossStatR",
  repos = c(
    rotsl = "https://rotsl.r-universe.dev",
    CRAN = "https://cloud.r-project.org"
  )
)
```

Alternatively, GitHub installation uses `remotes`:

```{r install-github, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("rotsl/crossStatR")
```

The package depends on `stats`, `MASS`, `Matrix`, `lme4`,
and `ggplot2` (all on CRAN). `nortest` is suggested for
Anderson-Darling normality testing but is not required.

## A quick example

Suppose the analyst has a small dose-response dataset with biological
replicates and two technical replicates per biological unit. The
honest analysis averages the technical replicates within each
biological unit first.

```{r quickstart}
set.seed(1)
df <- data.frame(
  y = rnorm(60, mean = rep(c(8, 10, 12), each = 20)),
  dose = rep(c("low", "mid", "high"), each = 20),
  bio = rep(1:6, each = 10),
  tech = rep(1:10, times = 6)
)
desc <- sci_describe(df$y, group = df$dose,
                     bio_rep = df$bio, tech_rep = df$tech)
print(desc)
```

The reported `n` per dose is the number of biological replicates after
collapsing the technical replicates. Compare with the naive call that
ignores the replicate structure:

```{r naive}
naive <- sci_describe(df$y, group = df$dose)
print(naive)
```

The naive call reports `n = 20` per group, which is misleading. The
standard errors are too small by roughly a factor of `\sqrt{2}` because
the within-bio correlation has been ignored. This is the standard
pseudo-replication failure mode and the reason `sci_describe()` asks
for the `bio_rep` argument.

A two-group comparison uses `sci_compare()` with the test the analyst can
defend a priori. The default is Welch's t; the documentation recommends Welch over
Student in essentially all experimental settings because Student's
pooled-variance assumption rarely holds for real measurements and the
Welch loss of power is small (Ruxton, 2006).

```{r compare}
x <- rnorm(12, mean = 10)
y <- rnorm(12, mean = 11)
sci_compare(x, y, test = "welch")
```

## Function catalogue

crossStatR ships 32 functions across three categories. See the
individual help pages for the mathematical details.

| Category | Function | Purpose |
|----------|----------|---------|
| A | `sci_describe` | Descriptive stats with bio/tech replicate separation |
| A | `sci_normality` | Shapiro-Wilk or Anderson-Darling with caveats |
| A | `sci_outliers` | IQR / MAD / z-score / robust-z flagging (no removal) |
| A | `sci_compare` | Welch / Student / permutation / Wilcoxon two-sample tests |
| A | `sci_anova` | ANOVA with effect sizes, Welch option, Tukey HSD |
| A | `sci_regression` | OLS / WLS / robust / nonlinear with measurement weights |
| A | `sci_correlation` | Pearson / Spearman / Kendall with Fisher-z CIs |
| A | `sci_bootstrap` | Nonparametric / parametric / cluster / stratified bootstrap |
| A | `sci_power` | Power and sample size with optional simulation check |
| A | `sci_effect_size` | Cohen's d, Hedges' g, paired d_z, r, partial eta-squared |
| B | `adaptive_baseline` | Asymmetric least squares or lowess baseline |
| B | `weighted_peak_fit` | Multi-peak NLS with Gaussian / Lorentzian / pseudo-Voigt |
| B | `adaptive_smoothing` | Savitzky-Golay / spline / lowess with PRESS window choice |
| B | `replicate_decompose` | Variance components via `lme4::lmer` REML |
| B | `drift_correct_stat` | Linear / polynomial / exponential drift with delta-method SE |
| B | `robust_lod` | Currie / blank-SD / Hubaux-Vos LOD with Monte Carlo CI |
| B | `calibration_compare` | ANCOVA comparison of two calibration curves |
| B | `curve_similarity` | L2 / L1 / DTW / correlation curve distance with CI |
| B | `kinetic_model_compare` | AIC/BIC comparison of candidate kinetic models |
| B | `spectral_change_test` | Hotelling T^2 / PERMANOVA / pointwise t for spectra |
| B | `noise_characterize` | Noise SD, ACF, heteroscedasticity, PSD, signal-dependence |
| B | `parameter_uncertainty` | Delta method / Monte Carlo / bootstrap propagation |
| B | `timepoint_optimize` | D / A / C / discrimination-optimal sampling times |
| B | `batch_effect_quantify` | LMM or fixed-effect batch variance decomposition |
| C | `signal_difference_regions` | Simultaneous confidence bands for curve differences |
| C | `peak_evidence` | Likelihood-ratio peak evidence with permutation null |
| C | `calibration_transfer_risk` | Transfer prediction error and OOD detection |
| C | `kinetic_discrimination` | Pre-experimental model discrimination probability |
| C | `experiment_fragility` | Sensitivity of results to analysis decisions |
| C | `drift_uncertainty` | Variance attribution to drift via bootstrap |
| C | `detection_reliability` | Concentration-dependent PD / FPR / FNR curves |
| C | `uncertainty_origin` | Shapley-style stage-wise uncertainty attribution |

Category A covers standard inferential and descriptive statistics,
wrapped with conservative defaults, effect-size reporting, and
bio/tech replicate handling. Category B contains domain-specific
signal-processing and calibration tools that overlap with packages
like `signal`, `pracma`, `chemCal`, and `driftR` but are unified under
the crossStatR calling convention. Category C contains eight diagnostic methods for signal comparison, calibration transfer, kinetic discrimination, fragility, detection, and uncertainty attribution. Their underlying statistical concepts overlap with established methods; no general claim of originality is made.

- Rochon, J., Gondan, M. and Kieser, M. (2012). To test or not to test: Preliminary assessment of normality when comparing two independent samples. BMC Medical Research Methodology, 12, 81. [Source](https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2288-12-81).

- Ruxton, G. D. (2006). The unequal variance t-test is an underused alternative to Student's t-test and the Mann–Whitney U test. Behavioral Ecology, 17, 688-690. [Source](https://doi.org/10.1093/beheco/ark016).

- Vaux, D. L., Fidler, F. and Cumming, G. (2012). Replicates and repeats—what is the difference and is it significant? The EMBO Reports, 13, 291-296. [Source](https://doi.org/10.1038/embor.2012.36).
